summary: A 1975 note examining how much of the response time in debugging programs across the network comes from ARPANET communication itself.

eli5.summary: If you test a program on a far-away computer, you wait for each answer. This note asks how much of that waiting is the network.

questions: how long does cross network debugging take
subtitle: How much delay does the ARPANET add to debugging?

tldr.problem: When a programmer at one computer debugs a program running on another computer over the network, the response delays matter. How much of the wait comes from the network itself?
tldr.mechanism: The X-NET debugger at BBN split the debugging work: the PDP-10 handles complex logic, the PDP-11 handles simple operations like examine and deposit. A test measured response times both locally and across the continent to SRI-ARC.
tldr.outcome: Network delays added about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds per command on average, comparable to typical time-sharing system delays. Cross-network debugging is practical.

today: RFC 685 is a record of early experience with cross-network debugging. The ARPANET has since evolved into the Internet, but the finding that network delay is tolerable for interactive work remains relevant.

sections.title: Cross-Network Debugging
sections.content:
A programmer can debug a program running on a distant computer by sending commands over the ARPANET and waiting for replies. The debugger at BBN split the work: the local PDP-10 handles complex logic such as symbol resolution, while the remote PDP-11 in the subject program's machine handles simple actions like reading and writing memory, setting breakpoints, and starting or stopping execution.

The key question is whether network communication adds enough delay to make this work tedious. This note reports on measurements taken during actual debugging sessions, comparing a local debug session with one that crossed the country to SRI-ARC in California.
sections.eli5: If you use a debugger on a computer across the country, is the wait unbearable? The team tested it to find out.

sections.title: The Test Scenario
sections.content:
The test ran 35 debug commands in a standard sequence: loading a program, starting and stopping execution, examining and modifying memory, setting breakpoints, and other typical debugging tasks. Each session lasted about 10 minutes. Measurements were taken on two days with the same scenario: once debugging a PDP-11 on the same IMP as the PDP-10 at BBN, and once debugging a PDP-11 at SRI-ARC in California with at least nine IMPs in the path.

The collected statistics track the size of messages and the total elapsed wait time (from handing the command to the network routines until receiving the reply). The time includes all network round-trips and asynchronous replies such as breakpoint notifications.
sections.eli5: The test used 35 real debugging commands. It measured how fast the computer answered when the debugger was next door versus when it was across the country.

sections.title: Response Time Results
sections.content:
For local debugging at BBN, the average wait per message was 1.75 seconds with a standard deviation of 2.04 seconds. For the distant site at SRI-ARC, the average was 1.89 seconds with a lower standard deviation of 0.78 seconds. The difference due to network distance is about 0.14 seconds on average.

The distribution of message sizes was bimodal: some commands like loading and word search transferred thousands of bytes, while others like start and stop needed only a few tens of bytes. Cache effects also mattered: subsequent examines of the same memory location were answered locally without network traffic.

The standard deviation is high partly because the test had a small sample size, but more importantly because debugging workloads vary widely. Some commands incur no network traffic when answered from cache, while others cross the network.
sections.eli5: The network added only about one-tenth of a second on average. The delays matched what you would see on a busy computer, not noticeably worse.

sections.title: Practical Feasibility
sections.content: The delays measured are tolerable. Network communication is of the same order of magnitude as delays that occur on moderately loaded time-sharing systems. The test did not break down delays into specific causes such as process activation, queueing, or IMP performance, but the overall result is clear: cross-network debugging is practical in use.
sections.eli5: Network debugging works fine in the real world. The wait is not so long that people mind doing it.
